Traditional ballad.note: In this setting any number of ABCB quatrains carry a third-person story on a returning tune, without a chorus. Dialogue and abrupt changes of scene are narrative devices available from verse to verse; neither has a fixed slot.

edges.evidence: The row explicitly puts successive ballad-stanza quatrains inside its narrative example.
In the illustrated version the narrative is carried by successive four-line units.

Long-measure ballad.note: The illustrated narrative quatrain has four stresses in every line. AABB is one rhyme arrangement. Dividing a regular fourteener into four and three stresses yields a different ballad-meter profile.

edges.evidence: A fourteener can break into four and three beats. That alternative belongs to a different metrical reading of the ballad, so it is excluded from the long-measure diagram.
The illustrated ballad stanza contains four four-stress lines. AABB is the catalog’s rhyme example; long metre alone does not determine rhyme.
Four lines in tetrameter match the long-metre profile when the feet are iambic. The source does not require every four-stress ballad line to be iambic.
A fourteen-syllable iambic line divided after eight syllables gives the four-and-three-stress profile of common metre, unlike the four equal lines shown.
The four equally stressed lines shown here differ from the alternating four- and three-stress lines of the traditional ballad stanza.

Ballad with internal refrain.note: A fixed refrain line recurs inside each stanza, interleaved with changing narrative or dialogue lines.

edges.evidence: The collected text places repeated lines inside changing narrative or dialogue stanzas.

Incremental-repetition ballad.note: Variants preserve a recurring verbal frame while changing phrases. A question-and-answer exchange can culminate in a final revelation; exact wording and ending vary.

edges.evidence: The collected variants repeat a verbal frame across exchanges while substituting details.

Broadside ballad.note: The broadside is a printed text. One topical layout opens by addressing listeners and closes with a moral. Singers could use a named tune, fit a different existing melody or supply their own. The tune choices apply to the whole printed text.

edges.evidence: Setting new ballad words to a named existing melody uses the same tune-reuse procedure. Printed broadsides also used other practices.

Come-all-ye.note: The initial address opens the narrative. A moral and a farewell are alternative endings, with no fixed stanza count supplied.

Goodnight ballad.note: First person is the narrator’s voice. The catalog places the warning within a confession and specifies a final farewell stanza.

Blues ballad.note: In this event narrative each stanza presents a fragment and ends with the returning refrain line. The next stanza can pick up another aspect of the event; no particular order of fragments is imposed.

Talking blues.note: The couplet or quatrain is half-spoken over the figure; the punchline closes that unit rather than adding a compulsory extra line.

edges.evidence: A rhymed couplet is one of the allowed vehicles for a half-spoken verse.
A quatrain is the four-line alternative in the same row.

Bothy ballad.note: The AABB story stanza has an optional following couplet. Scots work setting and comic subject describe the text, not additional sections.

edges.evidence: An optional two-line nonsense addition follows the AABB stanza.

Forebitter.note: Leisure singing aboard ship distinguishes the forebitter from a shanty used to coordinate work. A chorus is possible; the row leaves the size and ordering of its verses open. Section B names five shanties; this sixth maritime entry is explicitly a leisure song.

Cante fable.note: The sung verses interrupt the spoken narrative at significant moments. The row does not prescribe how many interruptions there are.

Mummers' play verse.note: In the rhymed hero-combat setting the characters introduce themselves, a fight leads to a death, a doctor revives the fallen character and a speech solicits a collection. This is one plot within mumming.

Calling-on song.note: The introductions name a dancer per stanza. A final call for the dance or for money is a choice of endings.

Luck-visit / begging song.note: Visiting singers may greet and bless a household, explain their custom and request provisions. In the illustrated wassail a changing verse ends with a repeated toast; the exact words vary later. Other visiting customs need not place a chorus there.

Street cry.note: The repeated unit is one sales phrase occupying one or two lines; an additional answer or verse is unspecified.

Dirge / lament.note: A documented funeral dirge places recurring responses inside each short stanza. The second and fourth lines recur around two changing lines. This illustrates one answer to the placement question within the much wider lament tradition.

edges.evidence: The illustrated funeral dirge uses a four-position mourning stanza in which the second and fourth positions recur.

Call-and-response.note: A leader’s line cues a group reply. In liturgical use this is responsorial; alternating choir groups exemplify antiphonal singing.

Halyard shanty.note: The hauling verse has two solo calls answered by the crew. A short full chorus can intervene before the next verse, in addition to the brief responses that coordinate the work.

edges.evidence: The shantyman’s line is answered by the crew in the halyard example.

Short-drag shanty.note: This short-haul example gives the solo line one brief group response. The stressed pull word is inside that response.

edges.evidence: A short crew reply answers one lead line and carries the pull cue.

Capstan shanty.note: The catalog pairs solo and crew lines inside a verse, with a larger chorus after the verse. Its use at a capstan identifies its function.

edges.evidence: The alternating solo and crew lines within the verse exhibit this vocal procedure.
In the catalog’s verse example, each solo line and answering crew line form an intentional two-line unit. The larger chorus follows the verse.

Stamp-and-go shanty.note: The row describes continuous alternating voices while the crew walks. It stipulates no verse boundary for this example.

edges.evidence: The walkaway description specifies a continuous succession of solo and group responses.

Pumping shanty.note: The response follows a solo couplet inside the longer pattern the catalog describes. Pumping is the work being done; an exact couplet length is an example.

edges.evidence: A chorus follows the lead singer’s couplets in the catalogued pumping example.
The row specifies that the chorus follows every solo couplet in this version.

Hammer song / chain-gang song.note: A lead line draws a fixed group response at the hammer stroke. AAB is a frequent textual pattern in the catalog. Its letters establish a return and change but do not determine which words are sung by each party or which letter coincides with the stroke.

edges.evidence: The responding workers time their fixed answer to the hammer stroke.

Field holler.note: The solo setting has freely timed calls and pauses without a stanza or chorus. A documented agricultural use adds an answering caller across a distance; the reply is optional and has no prescribed words.

Waulking song.note: The lead line and group answer on vocables repeat as a cycle. No count of cycles is specified.

edges.evidence: The waulking group answers its leader with vocables in each cycle.

Military cadence.note: The marching group echoes or answers the leader. Footsteps govern timing rather than adding a third musical section.

edges.evidence: The marching group repeats or answers the leader’s line in step.

Echo song.note: An echo is a verbatim group return of the leader’s words. No fixed verse length follows from that rule.

edges.evidence: The reply is the leader’s exact wording, a specific response rule.

Zipper song.note: An invariant frame and a substitution slot coexist within one verse. Only the word in that slot changes between iterations.

Cumulative song.note: The catalog illustrates newest-first recapitulation after adding each item. The entry supplies a progression, not an initial list length.

Counting song.note: The row explicitly calls this example cumulative. It accumulates numbered items, counts back to one and specifies a fixed closing tag.

edges.evidence: The row explicitly describes a cumulative number song that recalls earlier numbers, rather than every song used to teach counting.

Countdown song.note: A number goes down once per repeat of the same verse. Descending numbers alone do not imply accumulation of prior verses.

Riddle song.note: The answer stanzas follow the group of riddle stanzas in the same order in the described arrangement.

Nonsense-refrain song.note: The vocables belong to the refrain; the row does not give a line count or specify its exact position.

Lullaby.note: In the verse-and-refrain setting a soothing refrain frames short, softly delivered quatrains. This is a particular way to repeat material while soothing a child; four-line verses and a refrain are properties of this setting.

edges.evidence: The short verses of the catalog’s lullaby example are explicitly quatrains.

Nursery rhyme.note: The catalog gives a two- to eight-line range. Strongly accented quatrains commonly use AABB or ABCB. These rhyme choices describe the four-line examples; the source supplies no fixed rhyme for every other length.

edges.evidence: Each of the two complete four-line nursery-rhyme settings has the shape of a quatrain. The catalog also includes shorter and longer rhymes.
In the AABB quatrain, the first two and last two lines form two successive rhyme pairs. This claim is restricted to that branch.

Counting-out rhyme.note: The chant allocates one beat per child and ends on an elimination word. The word belongs to the chant’s ending.

Skipping / clapping rhyme.note: The strict rhythm applies to either couplets or quatrains. The counting or spelling tail is a separate closing unit. The choice of initial unit occupies one position.

edges.evidence: Strict-beat couplets are one of the alternatives before the tail.
Four-line verses are the other stated alternative before the tail.

Singing game.note: Each verse names an action, followed by a returning chorus between verses. The action is the verse content.

Finger play.note: Lines are paired with gestures. Body-part substitutions in later verses describe variation across repeats, not an extra section.

Dandling rhyme.note: The chant accelerates toward a closing drop line. The source gives a range of four to eight lines.

Playground taunt.note: The whole one- or two-line taunt repeats. No reply or fixed repeat count is given.

Tongue twister.note: Similar sounds crowd a one- to four-line text. Beyond that constraint the order of words and sections is open.

Dozens.note: Players trade ritual insults. Rhymed line pairs occur in the catalog’s verse example. Recorded practice also uses unrhymed speech.

edges.evidence: A rhymed line pair is one possible unit in the catalog’s verse example; the broader exchange does not prescribe paired lines.

Toast (oral narrative).note: A set opening leads to the recited narrative and a closing boast. Four-beat rhymed couplets are the narrative building blocks.

edges.evidence: The recited narrative is explicitly written in four-beat rhymed line pairs.

Square-dance singing call.note: A typical seven-part call has two figures before and two after the middle break. The catalog gives approximately 64 beats per part; an introduction or final tag can sit outside the seven parts. Dance calls fit the sung tune.

Square-dance patter call.note: Continuous dance instructions are spoken or rhythmically chanted to the beat over the music. The caller does not follow a fixed sung melody in this setting. Rhymed couplets are an option.

edges.evidence: A traditional realization fits a rhyming pair into the rhythmic call. This is optional for the wider practice.

Round.note: Delayed entries of a common melody overlap and can loop. A round is a looping kind of canon; the voices are concurrent once they enter.

edges.evidence: Voices enter in succession with the same melody and loop back, giving a perpetual canon.

Catch.note: The pun comes from words sounding together after staggered entries. The source identifies the catch as a comic round.

edges.evidence: The source calls a catch a comic round and locates the puns in its overlapping text.

Canon.note: One voice leads and another enters later in imitation. A strict canon preserves the leader’s material according to its rule; a free canon permits adjustments. A round cycles, while other canons may have a written close.

edges.evidence: A round illustrates looping canonic imitation. This reverse link points to a subtype, not a parent of canon.

Madrigal.note: In the illustrated English part-song a short lyric of six to twelve lines receives a continuously developing musical setting. The last text line is repeated. Repeating those words does not require repeating an entire musical section.

edges.evidence: The madrigal row explicitly calls the text setting through-composed. Its local repeat of a final line does not create a sectional return.
The row uses the broader term part-song. It supplies no evidence that this repertoire is a subtype of the specifically Victorian catalog entry.

Ballett.note: The half-stanza including its fa-la ending repeats; the repetition encloses both text and refrain. “Part-song” does not imply Victorian authorship or form.

edges.evidence: The row uses the broader term part-song. It supplies no evidence that this repertoire is a subtype of the specifically Victorian catalog entry.

Canzonet.note: Two or three voices and recurring stanzas with repeated sections characterize the catalog example. Voice count is a scoring detail, not a sequence.

edges.evidence: The canzonet description explicitly repeats its strophic setting while permitting internal repeated sections.

Ayre.note: In this strophic solo song with lute, the melody and stanza shape recur. One frequent rhyme option is ABABCC, with an alternating opening and a rhyming close; other settings need not follow that scheme.

edges.evidence: The same stanza design recurs in this voice-and-lute song.
The ABABCC option is a six-line verse unit in the repeated strophic setting.
The alternating ABAB opening is the four-line component of the optional ABABCC stanza.
The paired CC ending closes the illustrated ABABCC option.

Consort song.note: The strophic solo is accompanied by viols. The whole group enters for a repeat of the last lines in this account.

edges.evidence: The solo part is explicitly strophic; its final group return is a separate feature.

Three-man's song.note: Three voices sing successive stanzas with a refrain. Its position within the stanza is unspecified.

edges.evidence: Repeated music for successive stanzas is the common feature; the source also specifies a refrain.

Glee.note: An unaccompanied ensemble sings contrasting, through-composed sections. The number and order of contrasts are unspecified.

edges.evidence: The glee’s contrasting sections are explicitly described as a continuous through-composed setting.
The row uses the broader term part-song. It supplies no evidence that this repertoire is a subtype of the specifically Victorian catalog entry.

Part-song (Victorian).note: This entry explicitly identifies a Victorian setting with strophic chordal choir texture. The wider term part-song does not by itself establish a link to this subtype.

edges.evidence: This Victorian part-song row sets successive poem stanzas to recurring choral music.

Elizabethan stage jig.note: The stage jig uses ballad stanzas across several tunes. Changing tunes, characters and dancing are staging features rather than successive text units.

edges.evidence: The jig’s sung text uses ballad stanzas, even as tunes and characters change.

Medieval carol with burden.note: An opening two- to four-line burden precedes the first stanza and returns after each stanza. AAAB and AABB are alternative stanza rhymes.

Lullay carol.note: A lullay burden belongs to a cradle-song verse series. In one medieval example the parent and child take turns within the narrated verses; the burden recurs around the verse material. Versions differ in the extent of the child’s reply.

edges.evidence: The cradle-song setting and medieval carol share a recurring burden. The checked setting opens with the burden and marks it after its first stanza. The broader repertoire does not require all the same rhyme rules.

Christmas carol.note: The catalog offers hymn-like stanzas with a short refrain or a distinct chorus. A documented medieval Christmas setting places its burden after the stanza. That particular placement is one option within this seasonal repertoire.

Macaronic carol / song.note: The languages alternate within an otherwise independently chosen song design. A refrain is a possible switch point, not a required container.

edges.evidence: As defined in this catalog, the song is a sung instance of mixed-language verse, specifically alternating English and Latin. Other macaronic verse can use different languages.

Metrical hymn.note: Stanzas share a tune and a metrical profile. The linked metres are alternatives. Some settings close with a doxology.

edges.evidence: Metrical stanzas share a single tune; this describes repeated musical design rather than a complete identity of forms.
Four lines of 8, 6, 8 and 6 syllables form one possible hymn stanza.
Four eight-syllable lines form one possible hymn stanza.
Four lines of 6, 6, 8 and 6 syllables form one possible hymn stanza.
A doxology may serve as the last stanza of the hymn.
A hymn can combine two common-metre quatrains into one stanza.
One hymn stanza can extend long metre to eight eight-syllable lines.
A hymn can double the short-metre quatrain within one stanza.
A documented hymn stanza uses four six-syllable lines followed by two eight-syllable lines.
One attested hymn stanza uses doubled trochaic 8.7.8.7. This is an alternative to iambic hymn metres.
A strophic hymn may use another ordered syllable recipe. The catalog of recipes supplies alternatives for the stanza slot. The eight-line and single-stanza choices have independent profiles.

Hymn with refrain.note: A metrical stanza and the recurring refrain are successive units. The row does not give a specific hymn metre.

edges.evidence: A recurring refrain is appended to successive metrical hymn stanzas in this entry.

Gospel song (Sankey).note: In this revival-hymn setting each four-line verse leads to a returning four-line chorus carrying the title. The four-line count applies separately to the verse and the chorus.

edges.evidence: In this catalog example the verse and its title chorus each group four sung lines. Their rhyme and metre are unspecified.

Camp-meeting song.note: Some settings add a refrain to inherited hymn stanzas. The source allows it between stanzas or between lines and supplies no single required metre.

edges.evidence: A camp-meeting version may retain measured hymn stanzas and add a freely recurring refrain. The borrowing does not establish a single metre for the whole repertoire.

Praise chorus.note: The four- to eight-line stanza repeats several times before a closing tag. The tag sits outside the stanza repeat.

Spiritual.note: The catalog’s framed call-and-response setting is one possibility. Recorded traditions also include solo performance and choral arrangement; one documented quartet adds a chorus at the close. No common stanza design is inferred across them.

edges.evidence: The row’s group response follows the leader’s verse; this is a documented way to perform a spiritual.

Ring shout.note: A fixed group response follows an improvised leader’s line. The repeated cycle accelerates; acceleration is an attribute, not an extra passage.

edges.evidence: An improvised line and a fixed group reply form the repeating exchange.

Shaker gift song.note: The catalog repeats a four- to eight-line stanza. Dance is optional, and no musical position follows from its presence.

Table grace (sung).note: The base unit is one short rhymed stanza of thanks. It may be sung as a round, an optional performance treatment.

edges.evidence: The grace can optionally be performed as a round. This is a realization rather than a claim about all prayers before meals.

Ostinato chant (Taizé).note: The repeated chant and the cantor’s verses sound together; neither follows the other as a new section.

Metrical psalm.note: Two published paraphrases of the same psalm illustrate different stanza metres. Common metre alternates eight and six syllables; long metre has four eight-syllable lines. In either setting, successive stanzas can use one tune.

edges.evidence: One published setting gives successive quatrains in common metre.
An independently listed setting of the same text uses long-metre stanzas.
Several metrical stanzas can be sung to the same tune within a setting.
Both set metrical stanzas to a tune; the psalm paraphrase is specifically drawn from a scriptural psalm.

Lined-out hymn.note: The leader presents one line and the congregation sings that line back slowly. It is line-by-line participation rather than a separate verse and chorus.

edges.evidence: The leader provides one line for the congregation to return in song.

Anglican chant.note: Each half of a prose verse fits a portion of a recurring chant. In the illustrated pointing system a bar marks the change of measure and a dot divides syllables between its two halves. The verse text determines the syllables at each mark; this setting ends with a doxology.

edges.evidence: A doxology is the closing text of this example.

Psalm with antiphon.note: In this setting the antiphon opens, the two sides of the choir alternate verses, a doxology follows and the antiphon returns. The diagram identifies the framing positions of this particular setting.

edges.evidence: In this plan the doxology comes after the alternating verses and before the final antiphon.
Alternating choir sides and a leader answered by the group distribute the voices differently; an antiphon is the surrounding chant, not another name for the leader’s cue.

Responsorial psalm.note: The catalog response starts with the cantor and congregation and returns after the cantor’s verses. The Roman Mass also permits singing the psalm continuously, with the assembly listening and no intervening response.

edges.evidence: The congregation supplies the response between cantor verses in the responsorial option.

Responsory.note: The opening respond, verse and partial return form R–V–R′ in the entry. The second half belongs to the initial respond before it is reused.

edges.evidence: The initial response returns in part after the verse. The source explicitly marks the entry call/response; the exact performing forces are left open.

Litany.note: The fixed reply follows each separate petition. This models the recurring verbal unit rather than setting a number of petitions.

edges.evidence: A fixed response answers each of a succession of petitions.

Versicles and responses.note: An officiant’s versicle and the congregation’s answer form a recurring liturgical exchange. The wording can change from pair to pair.

edges.evidence: Leader and congregation take the two sides of each paired utterance.

The leader and congregation take successive turns in a liturgical exchange. The office prescribes the words and speakers without requiring that each utterance be a line of verse. The paired turns alone therefore do not establish a verse couplet.

Canticle.note: A fixed liturgical text can be chanted to a recurring formula or set to continuously developing music. The relevant office determines whether a doxology follows. These are independent choices of musical treatment and liturgical ending.

edges.evidence: The office prescribes a closing doxology for some canticles and omits it from others.
One musical treatment sets the fixed canticle text continuously, distinct from the chant-formula option.

Doxology.note: A short text of praise may stand alone or close a hymn. The catalog’s named examples differ in lineation, so four lines are illustrative.

edges.evidence: A doxology can serve as the hymn’s final stanza, a use explicitly permitted in both catalog rows. This points from the part toward its possible host.

Full anthem.note: A full choir sings the setting continuously. A closing acclamation appears in the illustrated arrangement. Full-choir scoring distinguishes this form from the alternating solo and choral passages of a verse anthem.

edges.evidence: The catalog describes its full-choir example as continuously setting a sacred text.
A full anthem can give the entire setting to the choir; a verse anthem can contrast solo and full-choir passages.

Verse anthem.note: Solo and full-choir passages alternate. “Verse” here marks solo scoring; the row does not identify a pop verse.

edges.evidence: Alternating solo and choir passages distinguish this setting from one written throughout for full choir.

Fuging tune.note: The first part of the hymn is sung together; staggered vocal entrances belong to the repeated second half.

Shape-note anthem.note: The scripture is set through, with chordal passages and imitative passages where the voices enter successively. These are types of texture available within an anthem. Passage order and count depend on the setting.

edges.evidence: The row describes the overall scripture setting this way even though its texture changes.
The catalog specifies imitative passages with successive vocal entries inside a longer anthem. That texture does not require a complete fuging tune as a component.

Mass setting (English).note: The five-part musical setting follows the customary Ordinary-text order. An English Communion rite can omit the song of praise, for example in Advent or Lent, or place it later in a different order of service. The complete rite includes other texts and actions.

edges.evidence: In this example the choir or cantor repeats a petition and the congregation answers. The final answer changes, so the strictly fixed-response litany describes only part of the design.

Anglican service.note: In the illustrated Evening Prayer selection two canticles follow separate lessons, each ending in a doxology. The office also permits other text selections. This diagram isolates the sung pair.

edges.evidence: The specific service setting consists of two separately identified canticles.
Each of the two canticles in this example ends in a doxology.
